The Ontology

Source: vignettes/overview-ontology.Rmd
overview-ontology.Rmd

The ontology is the shared catalog at the center of formex: a small, labeled map of every kind of column research data contains. Both halves of the package read it — guess_data_type() to decide where a column belongs, and fx_stabilize() to look up how to clean it. This guide walks the map one data type at a time.

How the map is organized

Every entry sits at four levels of increasing specificity:

data_type        how should it be treated?     number · text · temporal · ...
 └ semantic_family   what broad kind?           date · currency · geographic · ...
    └ semantic_type     what exactly?           calendar · usd · us_state · ...
       └ format_style / unit_type   how written / what unit?

The top level, data_type, is the load-bearing one: it decides whether a column is a quantity you can do math on, a label you must leave untouched, a point in time, and so on. The sections below are organized by it. Each opens with what the type is and how it differs from the types it is most often confused with, followed by the families and semantic types inside it.

The detector column

Not every type can be recognized just by looking at the values, and the ontology is honest about which can. Each type records how it is spotted, in a match_kind — shown as the detector column in every table below:

detector spotted by
genome a flexible date/time reader that tries many formats
mask a fixed written shape, sometimes with a self-checking digit
lexicon membership in a known list of allowed values
mask+lexicon the right shape and a match in a known list
shape the overall look of the numbers (range, decimals, sign)
none cannot be told from the values alone — only a name or data dictionary can

That last row matters for honesty. A membership-number column is just integers; a notes column is just text. No amount of looking at the values reveals what they are, so the ontology marks these none and the engine does not pretend.

data_type entries
boolean 5
categorical 13
identifier 10
number 23
structured 6
temporal 12
text 25
unknown 3

Those totals count geographic entries under their home data type (coordinates under number, GEOIDs under identifier, and so on); the final Geography section gathers them back together in one place.

number — quantities you can do math on

A number is a magnitude: something you can meaningfully add, average, or compare. This is the type to get right first, because it licenses arithmetic.

Not to be confused with identifier. A ZIP code, a county FIPS, and an account number are all written with digits, but they are labels, not magnitudes — averaging them is nonsense and dropping their leading zeros corrupts them. If digits are a quantity, they are a number; if they are a key, they are an identifier. The currency family carries a unit_type, because the same written number can mean dollars or euros. Geographic coordinates are numbers too — a lat/lon pair is a measurement on a datum — but they are gathered with the rest of geography in the Geography section at the end.

family semantic_type meaning formats / units detector
currency balance A signed account balance. balance
unit: USD 		mask
currency euro A euro amount (European format). euro
unit: EUR 		mask
currency usd A US-dollar amount. usd
unit: USD 		mask
portion odds Odds expressed as a ratio. odds shape
portion percent A percentage (0-100). percent shape
portion percentile A percentile position (0-100). percentile
unit: percentile 0-100 		shape
portion probability A probability (0-1). probability shape
quantity count A count of things. count shape
quantity duration An elapsed amount of time as a number. duration
unit: seconds;;minutes;;hours;;days;;years 		shape
quantity index A constructed index relative to a base. index
unit: index-specific scale 		shape
quantity measurement A measured value on a unit scale. measurement
unit: unit-specific (kg;;m;;C;;L) 		shape
quantity rank An ordinal rank position. rank
unit: rank position 		shape
quantity rate An amount per unit of exposure or time. rate
unit: per capita;;per 1,000;;per year 		shape
quantity ratio A ratio of two quantities. ratio
unit: numerator/denominator 		shape
quantity score A score on a defined scale. score

range min_max A low-high numeric pair. comma_pair, to_range
unit: same unit as estimate 		mask
* geographic geographic coordinates (lat / lon) are numbers — see the Geography section below

text — strings, from free prose to structured tokens

text covers values whose content is characters: names, email addresses, URLs, colors, and free-form notes. (Place names and postal addresses are geographic text, gathered in the Geography section at the end.) Some text is highly structured (an email, a hex color) and gets a scheme-specific recipe; some is genuinely free (text.long) and is simply preserved.

Not to be confused with categorical. A text column’s values are open-ended — a new row can introduce a name or note never seen before. A categorical column draws from a fixed, closed set of levels. “City name typed in freely” is text; “one of five survey response options” is categorical.

family semantic_type meaning formats / units detector
color cmyk A CMYK quadruple. cmyk mask
color color_name A named color (word), e.g. a hair or eye color. color_name lexicon
color hex A hex color. hex mask
color hsl An HSL triple. hsl mask
color rgb An RGB triple. rgb mask
contact email An email address. email mask
contact phone A phone number. phone mask
name handle A social / user handle. handle lexicon
name organization An organization’s name. organization lexicon
name person A person’s name. first_name, last_name, full_name lexicon / mask+lexicon
text label A short human label. label none
text literal Preserve raw data as-is. literal none
text long Long free text. long none
text serialized Serialized text (JSON/XML/delimited). serialized none
text title A title or heading. title none
web domain A domain / hostname. domain mask
web ip An IP address. ip mask
web mac A MAC address. mac mask
web url A URL. url mask
* geographic place names and postal addresses are text — see the Geography section below

temporal — points and spans in time

temporal values live on a timeline: a calendar date, a timestamp, a quarter, a day-of-week. They are detected by a flexible reader (genome) that recognizes many written forms and normalizes them to ISO. The period and phase families cover coarser or cyclic time (a fiscal quarter, a month-of-year), where a unit_type such as the fiscal convention can matter.

Not to be confused with number. 2019 could be a count or a year; 3.15 could be a measurement or a fragment of a date. What makes a column temporal is that its values locate something in time, which the reader confirms by parsing them as such.

family semantic_type meaning formats / units detector
date calendar A calendar date. calendar genome
date timestamp A date plus time of day. timestamp
unit: datetime;;timezone 		genome
interval date_range A date range. date_range
unit: date interval 		mask
period month A calendar month. month
unit: calendar month 		mask
period quarter A quarter. quarter
unit: calendar or fiscal quarter 		mask
period reporting_period A reporting period. reporting_period
unit: fiscal or reporting period 		mask
period year A year. year
unit: calendar or fiscal year 		mask
phase day_of_week A day of the week. day_of_week
unit: weekday position 		lexicon
phase hour_of_day An hour of the day. hour_of_day
unit: hour position 0-23 		mask
phase month_of_year A month of the year. month_of_year
unit: month position 1-12 		lexicon

categorical — a value from a fixed set of levels

A categorical column takes one value from a closed vocabulary: a Likert response, a classification code, a set of tags. The level-to-label mapping lives in a dictionary alongside the data; the ontology records only the shape of the encoding.

Not to be confused with boolean or text. A boolean is the special case of exactly two levels that mean true/false. Free strings with no fixed set are text. Many categorical types are none-detected: a column of codes 1, 2, 3 cannot be told from a count without its labels.

family semantic_type meaning formats / units detector
multiselect tags Zero or more levels per record. tags mask
mutually_exclusive classification_code A classification-system code. classification_code
unit: classification system & level 		mask+lexicon
mutually_exclusive missingness_reason A reason-for-missing code. missingness_reason
unit: missingness categories 		none
mutually_exclusive ordered An ordered (ordinal) category without intervals. ordered none
mutually_exclusive unordered An unordered (nominal) category. unordered none
scale grade_level An education grade level. grade_level
unit: ordered levels (K-12) 		none
scale likert A Likert agreement scale. likert
unit: ordered response scale 		none
scale ranking A ranking of options. ranking
unit: rank position 		none
scale rating A rating scale. rating
unit: ordered scale (1-5;;1-10) 		none
* geographic geographic groupings (state, country, city) — see the Geography section below

boolean — a two-state flag

A boolean is a yes/no, true/false, present/absent flag. formex recognizes a wide vocabulary of encodings (yes/no, t/f, 1/0, active/inactive, a bare x check) and maps them all to TRUE/FALSE.

Not to be confused with categorical. A boolean is exactly two states that collapse to logical true/false. Three or more mutually exclusive levels are categorical. The one thing that cannot be defaulted is the blank policy — a blank is missing in a survey but FALSE in a checkbox — so the encoding records it explicitly.

family semantic_type meaning formats / units detector
binary indicator A 0/1 indicator flag. indicator mask
binary mixed A mixed-encoding boolean (e.g. IRS 990). mixed mask
binary presence A present/absent (checkbox) flag. presence mask
binary response A yes/no survey response. response mask
binary status An on/off status. status mask

identifier — keys and codes that must be preserved exactly

An identifier labels something: an EIN, an ISBN, a DOI, a record key, a geographic GEOID (see the Geography section at the end). The defining rule is that its written form is the data — leading zeros, delimiters, and check digits all matter — so it must never be coerced to a number or silently reformatted.

Not to be confused with number. This is the most consequential distinction in the whole ontology, because treating an identifier as a number is how real data gets corrupted (06037 → 6037). Identifiers are detected by mask (a fixed shape, often with a checksum) and sometimes a lexicon of valid codes; record and entity keys are none, knowable only from context.

family semantic_type meaning formats / units detector
id administrative An administrative / registry ID. ein, isbn, doi, orcid, issn mask
id entity An entity identifier. entity mask
id hash A hash digest. hash mask
id record A record / row key. record mask
id version A version identifier. version mask
* geographic geographic keys (FIPS / GEOID) are identifiers — see the Geography section below

structured — composite values with internal parts

A structured value packs more than one field into a single cell: a JSON object, a WKT geometry (geographic geometries are gathered in the Geography section at the end), an array, a key-value blob. It is detected by the syntax of the container and is typically handled by parsing or splitting into component variables.

Not to be confused with categorical tags. A multiselect tag list is a flat set of labels; a structured value has real internal syntax (brackets, braces, coordinates) that a parser must honor.

family semantic_type meaning formats / units detector
collection array An array. array
unit: dimensions 		mask
collection list A list. list mask
record key_value A key-value mapping. key_value
unit: mapping 		mask
record object An object. object
unit: record schema 		mask
* geographic geographic geometries (point, polygon) — see the Geography section below

unknown — the honest fallback

unknown is where a column lands when the values cannot support any type: a column mixing dates, numbers, and prose (heterogeneous), a column of corrupt values (malformed), or one that simply did not resolve (unclassified). It is deliberately part of the ontology, so the engine always has a safe, truthful place to stop rather than forcing a wrong guess.

family semantic_type meaning formats / units detector
unknown heterogeneous A column mixing several data types. heterogeneous none
unknown malformed Malformed / parse-failure values. malformed none
unknown unclassified Unclassified values. unclassified none

geography — a cross-cutting domain, not a data type

Geography is the one case that deliberately does not get its own data_type, and it is worth saying why. The top level of the ontology classifies how a value should be treated, not what domain it is about — and a geographic value can need completely different handling depending on the column it sits in. The same place can be three data types at once: "Los Angeles County" the label, 06037 the key, and 34.3, -118.2 the coordinate.

So geographic entries are distributed across the data types above. Here they are gathered in one place, with a data_type column so the split is explicit:

data_type family semantic_type meaning formats / units detector
number coordinate lat A latitude. lat
unit: EPSG:4326 		mask
number coordinate lat_lon A lat/lon pair in degrees-minutes-seconds. dms, iso6709
unit: EPSG:4326 		mask
number coordinate lon A longitude. lon
unit: EPSG:4326 		mask
number coordinate lon_lat A lon/lat pair in degrees-minutes-seconds. lon_lat
unit: EPSG:4326 		mask
identifier id geographic A geographic key. geographic
unit: GEOID;;FIPS;;ZIP 		mask+lexicon
categorical mutually_exclusive geographic A geographic grouping. iso_country, us_state, us_city, county_fips
unit: geographic level 		lexicon / mask+lexicon
text name place A place / geographic name. place lexicon
text postal full A full postal address. full mask+lexicon
text postal po_box A PO box. po_box mask+lexicon
text postal street A street address line. street mask+lexicon
structured geometry point A point geometry. point
unit: EPSG:4326 		mask
structured geometry polygon A polygon geometry. polygon
unit: EPSG:4326 		mask

Why each case lands where it does:

  • number — coordinates. A latitude/longitude pair is a measurement on a datum (its unit_type is a coordinate reference system such as EPSG:4326). You interpolate it, compute distances, reproject it — all arithmetic — so it is a number.
  • identifier — geographic keys. A FIPS or GEOID like 06037 is a key you join on. Its leading zero and fixed width are load-bearing, so it must stay text and is hardened (FIPS-06037) against a spreadsheet silently turning it into 6037. Taking its average is meaningless.
  • categorical — groupings. A state or country used to group rows (us_state, iso_country) is a factor you analyze by: a closed vocabulary, matched against a lexicon.
  • text — place names and addresses. A freely typed city name or a street address is open-ended text — a new row can introduce one never seen before — so it is handled as text, not as a closed category.
  • structured — geometries. A WKT point or polygon packs coordinates into a single cell with real internal syntax that a parser must honor.

So when you meet a geographic column, the useful question is not “is this geography?” but “which treatment does it need?” — and the answer places it under the matching data type, with that type’s recipe for cleaning and storing it.

Stable identities, so a label means the same thing next year

Every entry carries a stable semantic_type_id (like n0059) and variant_id (like n0059-f01) that are assigned once and never reused. Types are retired rather than deleted, so a label you record today still means the same thing years from now. fx_ontology() reads the whole map; fx_validate_ontology() checks it is internally consistent.
